Integrated-Gradients attribution diversity was 2.3 times greater in fusion-rescued cases. Removing divergence-driving words destroyed 58% of rescues, versus 12% under random removal. These findings show that lineage auditing detects dependencies missed by lexical filtering, while class-specific complementarity and post-fusion calibration reveal ensemble behavior obscured by aggregate accuracy.

title: CausalGloss: Multi-Evidence Action Control for a Simultaneous Mandarin Speech-to-ASL Gloss Cascade
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
summary: Simultaneous Mandarin speech-to-American Sign Language (ASL) gloss translation requires deciding when an evolving utterance supports committing each gloss. Fixed Wait-k cannot adapt to source-gloss reordering, while training only on reference histories causes exposure bias. We present CausalGloss, an English-prefix-to-ASL-gloss action policy for a Mandarin-speech cascade. It combines lexical and semantic evidence, bounded delay, negation constraints, burst WRITE actions, and incomplete-history recovery. On a frozen 500-example How2Sign-derived benchmark with weak LLM-generated references, CausalGloss improves the fixed Wait-k frontier and nearly matches a three-seed TransLLaMA-style learned adaptive baseline at k = 5 in Token F1 (0.7047 versus 0.7067), with 54.4% lower LAAL. Against CLERC Epee human-gloss references, it achieves 0.649 Token F1 and Pareto-dominates three-seed TransLLaMA-style k = 5 and fixed k = 5, 7, reducing LAAL by 58.2-69.9%. Ablations separate timing from retention. A synthetic Mandarin-speech cascade preserves a smaller computation-aware latency gain, although outputs remain over-long. We also construct ChineseSpeech-ASLGloss-v1, a 19,924-utterance, 36.54-h controlled evaluation corpus.

title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
summary: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

title: Real-World End-to-End Product Entity Resolution
summary: Product Entity Resolution (PER) in e-commerce is challenging due to unstructured text, formatting inconsistencies, promotional noise, and fine-grained product differences. We present an end-to-end evaluation of four zero-shot PER pipelines---Lexical Cascade, Semantic Cascade, Hybrid Fusion Cascade, and Generative-Lexical Cascade---across established benchmarks and introduce two real-world datasets characterized by cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions. We evaluate lexical and dense blocking with cross-encoder, tensor-search, and Large Language Model verification, considering accuracy, runtime, and memory consumption.

title: Do Rule-Based Tools Help LLMs Translate Endangered Uralic Languages in the Prompt or over MCP?
comment: Accepted at the 11th International Workshop on Computational Linguistics for Uralic Languages (IWCLUL 2026), Munich. 9 pages plus appendices, 1 figure, 10 tables. Data and all model outputs: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Aragoner/UralicMCPBench
summary: Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya and Udmurt have mature rule-based resources, among them finite-state analysers, constraint grammars and bilingual dictionaries, which language models do not use. We ask whether giving a model access to these resources improves machine translation from the four languages into English, and whether it matters how the access is provided: as analyses computed in advance and written into the prompt, or as tools that the model calls itself through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We evaluate manually: an expert linguist read every English output of the strongest model under three conditions, 816 sentences in all, accepted or rejected each one, and named the main error in every rejected translation. With the analyses in the prompt, the number of accepted translations rises from 13 to 43 out of 272; with the tools attached it rises to 55. The gain comes from the bilingual dictionary. For Udmurt, whose dictionary has no English side, the prompt-based condition brings no gain at all, while for the other three languages an English gloss reaches the prompt for 74 to 80% of the source words. Tool calling is also much harder to get working than prompt injection. Of 31 open-weight models, 14 never call a tool, 11 of them because they cannot produce a usable call, and half of the calls that are made name a language the toolkit does not support. We release the data set, every model output and all tool-call logs.

title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
summary: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Unifying Representations in Neural Models (UniReps) co-located with NeurIPS 2026.(arXiv preprint)
summary:
A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator.
  The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
summary: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

title: Formalizing Formal Semantics: The Formal Atlas
summary:
In this paper we present the Formal Atlas, a system for the study of natural language semantics using proof assistants. Our aim is to formalize semantic accounts,
  check their predictions and compare the implemented theories. To this end, we connect source records and formal developments with an interactive application, where
  researchers can inspect proofs and modify supported Rocq files. Montague's PTQ and Gallin provide our main cases, followed by dynamic and type-theoretic
  comparisons, RSA and distributional semantics. We also discuss what it takes to formalize less explicit analyses. Lastly, we consider the use of AI, both for
  assistance in developing these resources and for inference systems that can make use of them. This work extends an earlier programme in proof-assistant semantics,
  with research and teaching as complementary uses.

title: Sada-ASR: A Production Multidialectal Arabic Speech Recognition System
summary: Callers to Arabic customer-service lines speak their own dialect, while speech recognizers are built and evaluated mainly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). A recognizer that mishears the dialect breaks the call before anything else can help. We present Sada-ASR, the speech recognizer of EchoNova's production Arabic voice agent. On a 120-hour test set of MSA and eight dialects, it has the lowest word and character error rates of twelve systems, against eleven from Microsoft, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Speechmatics, IFM, Cohere, NVIDIA and Audar: 11.69% word error rate against 13.51% for the strongest, Microsoft's MAI-Transcribe-2 (a lead of 0.74 points on clips unaffected by that system's fixed number and script conventions), and 15.52% against 16.96% averaged over varieties. Its largest margins are on Omani (4.30 points), Egyptian (3.78) and Saudi (2.19) speech; it is level on Syrian and loses on Lebanese (24.96% against 23.05%), mostly because it writes Lebanese words in MSA forms and is less verbatim. On six public test sets its average word error rate under the leaderboard's current scoring is 17.17%, below every published figure we found, among them Falcon-ASR (20.92%), Jais-ASR (22.85%) and Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%), though none of these states that it used that scoring, so the comparison is indicative. We describe the data pipeline and methodology behind Sada-ASR and release a 20-hour subset of the test set with our scoring code.

title: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Proceedings Track; to appear in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR). 17 pages
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
summary: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

title: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. 39 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/thenexuslab/stalebench-release
summary: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.

title: Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA
comment: 37 pages, 30 figures, 20 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2027. Code: https://github.com/PaulKMandal/dataset-cartography-qa
summary: Dataset cartography argues that training dynamics can reveal regions of a dataset that matter differently for learning: easy-to-learn examples aid optimization, hard-to-learn examples often expose annotation problems, and ambiguous examples contribute strongly to out-of-distribution generalization. A striking implication of the original work is that a model trained on only 33% ambiguous examples can outperform full-data training on several OOD evaluations, including a QNLI reformulation of SQuAD evaluated on Adversarial SQuAD. We revisit this claim in a stricter setting: open-ended extractive question answering, where models must predict answer spans rather than classify question-sentence pairs. For each encoder family, we compute clean-source SQuAD training dynamics, train on full, random, easy-ranked, ambiguous-ranked, and hard-ranked subsets, and evaluate robustness on adversarial-only AddSent and AddOneSent rows. Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets on exact-match accuracy in all 14 model-evaluation cells and on F1 in 12/14 cells. However, full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, with mean full-minus-ambiguous gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1. The most thoroughly replicated ELECTRA-small panel is also the main exception to the ambiguous-over-random F1 gains. These results show that clean-source cartography remains useful for reduced-data selection, but its OOD advantage does not carry over as a general replacement for full-data training in extractive adversarial QA.

title: Logical AI OS: A Training-Free Governance Layer Outside the Model for Instruction Following -- Benefits, Costs, Failures, and the Calibration of the Measuring Instrument Itself
comment: 18 pages, 5 tables, 3 figures. Technical report v3. Earlier reports in this line: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23226740 (Measurement Layer) and the Validation Layer report. Data, model answers, per-item verdicts, annotations and the standalone checker: https://github.com/blackwing04/Logical-AI-OS (tag v3.0-data). The governance-layer implementation is not released
summary: Small language models often fail explicit user requests (length, number of items, format, required or forbidden words, grammatical person, answer language). We measure a training-free governance layer placed outside the model: it reads the requests with rules, checks the answer mechanically, repairs it when a request is not kept, and hands back the original answer when the repair fails. The loop exists in prior work; our contribution is measuring its benefits, costs and failures, and reporting how the measuring instrument itself was calibrated. On four 4-bit Qwen-family models (3B, 7B, 14B, one 7B reasoning model) and 329 Chinese prompts: (1) answers that keep every request the layer read rise significantly (all comparisons p<0.0001), by 34 to 66 of 329 under the corrected checker and 52 to 92 after a length-control fix; a generic redo message brings no significant gain. (2) Exploratory: on 90 repair-triggered prompts, two AI annotators found the layer produced an acceptable answer where the bare model did not more often than the reverse (49:7; 18:12, not significant). (3) Costs: 43-66% more generation time; whole-answer rewriting makes a sizeable share of usable answers unusable. (4) Failures: rule-based reading reaches about 70% and 84% of a two-annotator ceiling on unseen phrasings; unsatisfiable requests make the reasoning model loop; model self-reports are unreliable (18 of 25 "fixed" items were not fixed). (5) Over half of the original checker's "violated" verdicts on structural requests were wrong; after correction the main result holds, and one comparison is downgraded. Conclusions are limited to this Chinese material, the Qwen family and sizes up to 14B. The governance implementation is not released; data, answers, verdicts and the checker are public.

title: Machine interpreting competitiveness: a discourse-sensitive comparison of meaning and target-language quality in English-Chinese simultaneous interpreting
comment: 88 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Includes Supplementary Information (40 pages)
summary: Machine interpreting (MI), or AI-enabled speech translation, is increasingly visible in professional and public-facing communication, yet its performance relative to human simultaneous interpreters remains insufficiently understood. Existing studies are often limited by a single discourse mode and evaluation frameworks that are not well aligned with interpreting as a discourse-level communicative activity. The present study compares five commercial MI systems with 26 human interpreters (14 professionals, 12 advanced students) on English-to-Chinese simultaneous interpreting across planned and unplanned discourse, focusing on meaning and target-language quality. In these materials, MI performance differed sharply between the two discourse modes. In the planned formal speech, the strongest system became highly competitive on meaning, entering the upper human range, and a second system also performed strongly. In the extemporaneous interview, however, no MI system approached the stronger human tiers. Code-level analysis further shows that similar overall scores often masked different error profiles. Human interpreters were more likely to preserve the broader communicative trajectory through selective omission, restructuring, and contextual inference, whereas even the best MI systems were more vulnerable to semantic distortion, discourse-tracking failures, and context-insensitive interpretation. On target-language quality, the human advantage proved more stable than on meaning. Unintelligible or nonsensical output and disfluency carryover emerge as particularly salient weaknesses in machine performance, especially in spontaneous discourse. Overall, the findings are consistent with a discourse-sensitive account of where MI appears competitive, where it remains limited, and why these distinctions matter for interpreting practice, interpreter education, and future MI development.

title: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
comment: 11 pages, 2 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24237533
summary:
Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is imperceptible in double-blind evaluation by both humans (8/16) and a calibrated LLM judge (9/16).
  A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; single-text 22/24, same-topic pairs 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swapping, counting disagreement as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 [0.699, 0.972], repetition 0.114 to 0.000, unchanged MMLU. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains, w=0.3 does not). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
summary: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation
summary: As globalization accelerates the demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration, multilingual translation remains bottlenecked by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following capabilities, and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. To overcome these barriers, we propose Bridging the Terminology Gap (BTG), a data-centric framework. First, BTG mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and leverages LLMs to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. Second, a hybrid filtering strategy combining heuristics and XCOMET scoring ensures high data fidelity. Third, a two-stage training paradigm employs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for targeted terminology injection, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to refine output preferences, effectively balancing domain knowledge integration with model reliability. Extensive offline evaluations (e.g., XCOMET, GEMBA, Acc@T) and online human assessments demonstrate significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities, validating the effectiveness of our framework, which is now deployed on our cross-border collaboration platform.

title: Bioformer-RetroMAE: retrieval-oriented pretraining of a compact biomedical language model for literature search
summary: Dense retrieval is increasingly used for biomedical literature search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Most biomedical bi-encoders are built on BERTBase-sized encoders pretrained with masked language modeling (MLM). These encoders are costly for corpus-scale indexing and latency-sensitive query encoding, and MLM does not explicitly train the [CLS] vector that a bi-encoder uses to represent a whole text. We present Bioformer-RetroMAE, a compact (43M-parameter) retrieval-oriented biomedical encoder obtained by continually pretraining Bioformer8L} with RetroMAE on approximately 32 million PubMed titles and abstracts. After bi-encoder fine-tuning with BM25 hard negatives, we evaluated it on BioASQ Task 12B test questions by retrieving from all PubMed abstracts. Bioformer-RetroMAE outperformed BioBERT and PubMedBERT bi-encoders fine-tuned under identical settings on all metrics, despite having about 40% of their parameters and producing 512-dimensional rather than 768-dimensional vectors. Compared with PubMedBERT, it improved mean average precision (MAP) by 37.0% and Recall@100 by 29.1%. Compared with the original Bioformer8L}, RetroMAE pretraining improved MAP by 53.6% and Recall@100 by 32.8% without changing model size or inference cost. In hybrid retrieval, fusing Bioformer-RetroMAE with BM25 through weighted reciprocal rank fusion improved MAP and NDCG@10 over BM25 alone by 4.9% and 4.6%, respectively, larger gains than those obtained by fusing BM25 with PubMedBERT or BioBERT.

title: Attribute or Abstain: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Retrieval on the Low-Resource African Business Web
summary: Retrieval-augmented systems that research companies are judged by how much they find, yet in markets where public evidence is sparse, a confident answer without support costs more than no answer. We introduce AfriBizClaims, a benchmark of 150 company-research queries across six African markets in English, French and Portuguese, including queries about fictitious companies that a correct system must decline. Each claim a system makes is judged against the page it cites by an AI judge, checked against a second AI judge from another model family and against two human annotators, and abstentions are scored against answerability labels. We compare BM25 over a pooled corpus, standard web retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-step agent pipeline (Konexium V1), all using the same language model. The two simple baselines are well attributed: 98% of their judged claims are supported by the page they cite, and they decline every field of every fictitious company. Counting claims about a company other than the one asked about as errors, the agent pipeline's per-query precision is 68%, and it never answers a question about a named company correctly: it substitutes other firms, including for 5 of the 24 fictitious names, and it is the least stable between runs and the most expensive. In the pipeline we evaluated, more steps between the query and the evidence did not buy more grounded answers. We will release the queries, system outputs, labels and short evidence excerpts.

title: The Vocabulary Tax: Safely Trimming Unused Tokens from LLMs for On-Device Use
summary: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.

title: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
summary: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
comment: Empirical study with an original dataset: 40 LLM technical reports coded by two independent model coders with script-verified quotes, plus a code-level comparison of open-weight architectures in Hugging Face transformers. 20 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Data, coding protocol and scripts in the ancillary files
summary: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
summary: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.

title: A Dataset for Misogyny Detection in Polish Social Media: Transferability of Hateful Speech Detection from General to Specific Types of Hate
summary: Harmful language detection is commonly evaluated on broadly defined hate speech and toxicity benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether models that successfully detect harmful language in general can transfer this capability to more specific forms of hate. We investigate this problem for misogyny detection in Polish, an area for which dedicated resources remain scarce. We introduce a new dataset of Polish social media comments annotated for misogyny, gender-directed hateful speech. Using this resource, we first assess the reliability of LLM-assisted annotation and then evaluate general-to-specific transfer by comparing models trained on general harmful language data, safety-specialized models, and models fine-tuned directly for misogyny detection. Our results show that strong performance on general harmful language detection does not transfer uniformly to misogyny; safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization ability. The study contributes a new Polish resource for gender-directed harmful language and demonstrates that the scope and granularity of prior safety training are important factors in transferring harmful language detection from general to specific forms of hate.

title: Mandarin Wh-Indefinites Follow Nonveridicality in Multilingual LLMs, Unlike English any
summary: Multilingual LLMs learn mostly from English. Do they carry English polarity licensing over to other languages? English any is licensed by downward-entailing (DE) contexts, Mandarin wh-indefinites such as shenme 'what/something' by nonveridical ones, and the two classes come apart: perhaps licenses shenme but not any, while only licenses any but entails existence. We test this dissociation in a pre-registered study of twelve open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families), using 48 matched bilingual frames in 21 contexts and a log-probability difference-in-differences normalised by negation. All 11 models that pass the measurement gate license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity and evidential adverbs, at 0.42-2.33 times the strength of negation, while English any gets nothing in the same contexts. An exploratory extension to Qwen2.5-32B shows the same. The English side is weaker: any under only, first and regret is licensed but at a fraction of negation, so only 3 models show the full double dissociation in sentence probabilities. When prompted to choose between sentences, most gated models show it. In exploratory directional ablations, a direction that carries English licensing, held-out classes included, does not reach Mandarin licensing in most models. The models do not simply apply the English rule to Mandarin.

title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

title: FRAAC: A French Multimodal Large Language Model and Dataset forPictogram-Based Augmentative and Alternative Communication
summary: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.

title: A Corpus-Driven SentencePiece Unigram Tokenizer for Sindhi: Design and Benchmark Against Fourteen Existing Tokenizers
comment: 13 pages; code and tokenizers at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23962474
summary: Sindhi is a low-resource Indo-Aryan language written mainly in an extended Perso-Arabic script. Several Sindhi tokenizers have been released on public model hubs, but they have not been compared with one another on shared data. We train SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers with byte fallback at four vocabulary sizes (32k to 150k) on about 1.10 million Sindhi sentences and a smaller, repeated Urdu, Persian and Arabic slice, from four public sources, and compare them with fourteen existing tokenizers on four evaluation sets: FLORES+, Sindhi Wikipedia, a news-derived sentiment corpus, and a contemporary news corpus. The metrics are fertility, single-token retention, UNK rate, byte-fallback rate, and round-trip character loss. At 64k, our tokenizer averages 1.147 tokens per word, against 1.208 for the best existing tokenizer and 1.512 for XLM-RoBERTa, and keeps 88.6% of words as single tokens. On fertility, single-token retention and UNK rate it is best or tied for best in all four evaluation sets at 64k and above; at 32k it trails one baseline on FLORES+. Margins over the best Sindhi-adapted baselines are small (0.002 fertility on FLORES+ at 64k), and we report no significance tests. A round-trip check finds no character loss for our tokenizer and silent character deletion (up to 0.85% of characters) in two existing ones; seven others lose less than 0.1%. We evaluate intrinsic metrics only, so effects on downstream tasks remain untested. Code and tokenizer files are public (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23962474).

title: Can decision models extract clinical data from cancer pathology reports? An evaluation of accuracy, calibration, and failure modes
summary: Decision models are a new class of language model that, instead of generating text, choose one option per question from a fixed list and return a probability for every option. They have not yet been evaluated on clinical text. We evaluated two open-weights decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, for extracting 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports from a single centre, against a prospectively maintained clinical database. We compared them with two generative models: Qwen3.5 9B, run locally, and GLM-5.3-flash, run through a cloud API. Tev1 reached a mean field accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI 0.913 to 0.920), the same as Qwen3.5 9B (0.918; p = 0.26), and was four times faster (15 s against 61 s per report). Nimble reached 0.862 and GLM-5.3-flash 0.986. Both decision models matched GLM-5.3-flash on simple dichotomous categories. They were weak on measurements binned into categories, on fields whose correct answer was not reported, and on some complex decisions (e.g. involved margins). We found that the main cause of the inferior performance of Nimble's came from asking 25 questions in one request: with two questions per request, its accuracy improved. Pooled over fields, the returned probabilities were well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.022 and 0.026), but they did not flag systematic errors within single fields. A simulated strategy of sending answers with a probability below 0.94 to GLM-5.3-flash raised Tev1's accuracy to 0.982, with 38% of answers escalated. Decision models can extract explicitly stated findings from pathology reports quickly on local hardware and return useful probabilities. They should be validated in the configuration in which they will be used, restricted to the fields in which they are reliable, and combined with other methods for numeric values.

title: Rank, Don't Regress: A 279M Text Ranker Beats 2B and 7B VLMs on Referential Urdu GUI Grounding
summary: UI grounding asks a model to find the screen element that a user instruction refers to. Most current systems use a vision-language model (VLM) that reads a screenshot and outputs pixel coordinates. We study this task on Urdu mobile web pages, a setting with no published UI grounding results. Instead of regressing coordinates, we take the candidate elements from the page DOM and train a 279M-parameter cross-encoder (mDeBERTa-v3-base) to pick one. The click point is the centre of the picked element's box, so it is exact whenever the right element is picked. We built a frozen test set of 304 instructions from six Urdu news sites; 149 of them (49%) are referential and never quote the full target text. Test domains were banned from training data before collection started. The ranker scores 73.4% point-in-box accuracy, against 29.6% for UI-TARS-2B and 23.7% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both zero-shot. On the referential slice the ranker scores 65.8%, against 30.2% for a string-matching baseline that needs no training. In a controlled comparison at small scale, with training data drawn from the same pages, a coordinate-regression model of similar size scores 1.6%. Adding element geometry as input tokens gives the best variant, at 75.7%. The ranker's errors concentrate in two places: elements that share identical text, and ordinal instructions such as "the fourth link".

title: Centered Ablation: Why Last-Layer Directional Ablation Under-Fires or Collapses, and a Closed-Form Fix
summary: Directional ablation removes a hidden state's component along a "behaviour direction" while a language model runs. It is the standard way to switch a behaviour such as refusal off, but it is erratic: on some models it barely fires, on others the text collapses into repetition. We show why, and fix it. At the last residual stream, ablation is exactly a logit bias: a fixed vocabulary footprint scaled by a gate, the cosine between the hidden state and the direction. The gate is measured from the origin, but last-layer states share a large common mode far from it, so a direction that overlaps the common mode fires on benign text and under-fires on its targets. Centered Ablation (CA) projects the common mode out of the direction, in closed form. Across 8 models, CA raises attack success by 29 and 46 points where the standard recipe under-fires, cuts collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50\% to 1\%, and preserves 12 to 40 points more benign answers on high-overlap models, 39 to 46 more than the affine offset of prior work. Two numbers computed before generation predict, on models the analysis had not seen, which gain faithfulness and which gain attack success, and a collapse index marks when text degenerates. We also show that two standard safety judges score collapsed text in opposite directions, which can fabricate a 46-point effect.

title: Risk-certified prompt optimization for LLM-as-a-judge guardrails
summary: LLM-as-a-judge guardrails are often controlled primarily through system prompts, yet standard prompt optimization methods target average performance rather than explicit safety constraints. This paper studies system-prompt selection as a constrained optimization problem: maximize benign pass rate while keeping the missed-attack rate below a user-specified level α with finite-sample statistical control. The framework combines LLM-based judging, automatic prompt generation, and distribution-free risk certification. This work instantiates it in two procedures: CPS and CRISP. CPS generates a fixed pool of prompts from training data, then certifies candidates on a held-out evaluation set using simultaneous upper confidence bounds and selects the certified prompt with the highest benign utility. CRISP instead integrates risk feedback into an adaptive search, using hard example-guided rewriting and a reusable-holdout interface to steer generation toward the feasible utility frontier. Experiments on four datasets covering prompt injection, system-prompt leakage, and sensitive-information disclosure show that risk-certified selection consistently respects the target missed-attack level on heldout tests, while utility improves as the permitted risk is relaxed. CRISP is especially useful when fixed-pool search fails to produce certifiable high-utility candidates.

title: Who Can You Hide Behind? Author-Conditioned Style Transfer and the Evasion of a Commercial AI-Text Detector
summary: AI-text detectors can be sensitive to changes in writing style. We examined this sensitivity by rewriting 991 AI-generated answers with Gemini, using prompts that included a writing sample from one of 55 named authors. We scored each original and its rewrite with the QuillBot AI detector. The median score fell from 100% to 0%, and the mean fell from 67.9% to 11.2%. Of the rewrites, 66% received a score of exactly 0%. Among the 699 originals scored at least 50%, 71% of rewrites scored below 10% (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p-value below 1e-100). Scores varied across the authors used in the prompts. All rewrites associated with 10 authors scored 0%, whereas the mean score remained above 50% for six authors (Kruskal-Wallis test, p-value below 1e-80). Greater reuse of five-word sequences from the author sample was associated with lower scores, although rewrites with less than 5% reuse still averaged 15.2%. These results describe one detector and one rewriting system, not detectors in general. The study lacks a generic-rewrite baseline, did not measure preservation of meaning, and produced rewrites that were substantially longer than the originals.

title: Do We Still Need Fine-Tuned Classifiers? Swapping Typed Decision Models into 24 ACL-Venue Papers
summary: Typed Decision Models such as TypeSafe's Jev, also called System One or System 1 models, answer typed questions about an input with a probability for each option, and they need no training. Many NLP papers still fine-tune a task-specific classifier, and prompted large language models (LLMs) trail such classifiers on most text classification benchmarks. We ask how many of these fine-tuned classifiers a Typed Decision Model can replace under each paper's own evaluation, and what is needed where it cannot. We swap the predictors of 24 ACL-venue papers for Jev, keep each paper's splits, label definitions and metric, and check the results with Cloudflare's Clef, Microsoft-Decision-1 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna Decisions. The resulting 46 English test sets, with their questions and published scores, form the TDM-Gauntlet benchmark. With a zero-shot prompt, Jev directly replaced the paper's predictor on 12 of the 46 test sets, mostly single judgments with plain labels, but rarely where the paper's method was trained on its labels. Where Jev scored lower, we most often attributed the shortfall to an annotation convention that the label name does not state. With 500 training labels plus validation and no user-managed GPU, calibration and GEPA-style prompt optimization closed a median 72% of the gap to the paper's method, about twice what off-the-shelf GEPA closed, for a median $1.66 per search. On the same labels, fine-tuned encoders such as RoBERTa and DeBERTa closed 59%, and LoRA fine-tuning of the open LLM Qwen3.8-27B closed 97%. Fine-tuning remains the most accurate option, but a zero-shot prompt is often enough for plain labels, and prompt optimization closes most of the remaining gap.

title: FIDEL: Abugida-Aware Pre-tokenization for Ethiopic Languages
summary: Subword tokenizers assume that meaningful linguistic units can be recovered by splitting text at learned boundaries, an assumption better suited to concatenative morphology than to Semitic root-and-pattern systems. The challenge is acute for the Ethiopic languages, whose abugida script encodes consonant-vowel units as single characters and hides consonantal structure. We introduce FIDEL (FIdäl DEcomposition and Linearization), a family of reversible abugida-aware pre-tokenization schemes that expose consonant and vowel-order structure, extend SPLINTER reductions from abjad scripts to the Ethiopic abugida, and evaluate them on three Ethiopic languages under controlled conditions, holding corpus, architecture, budget and protocol fixed so that tokenization is the only variable. We report intrinsic tokenizer statistics for BPE and UnigramLM across vocabulary sizes alongside downstream NLP tasks, including transfer scenarios. We find that FIDEL reduction improves news classification consistently and named-entity recognition at larger capacity, while sentiment analysis performance declines under the more aggressive schemes, and extractive question answering performance is preserved.

title: Hochschild Cocycle and Universality of Merge
summary: The Hopf algebra Markov chain dynamical system, on the Hopf algebra of non-planar binary forests, that models the action of Merge on workspaces in Chomsky's Minimalist Model of syntax, satisfies a universal property, determined by the fact that the Merge operation is a Hochschild 1-cocycle. This universal property has an interpretation in terms of models of the syntax-semantics interface, as it shows that, if the side of semantics possesses a sufficiently rich compositional structure, then that structure is uniquely induced by the syntactic Merge, once the semantic values of lexical items and syntactic features are assigned. We illustrate how this universality works by showing, in particular, full compatibility of this Hopf algebraic formulation with Heim-Kratzer semantics.

title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
summary: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.

title: Refusal Register is Causally Steerable: Decomposing the Refusal Direction into Category-Aligned Components in Gemma-2-9B-IT
summary: Prior work shows that refusal in instruction-tuned language models can be ablated by intervening on a single residual-stream direction (Arditi et al., 2024), and more recent work finds multiple refusal-mediating directions and concept cones (Wollschläger et al., 2025). We ask a different question: do refusal-related directions carry information about the register of refusal language - how the model refuses - and not only whether it refuses? In Gemma-2-9B-IT we identify two SVM-derived linear directions (B1 for harmful-content vs. neutral, B2 for self-reference vs. neutral) at layer 20 with cos(B1, B2) = 0.252 (about 75 degrees, substantially non-parallel). Adding the harmful-vs-neutral difference-of-means direction (cosine 0.68 with B1) to the residual stream of self-reference prompts at alpha = 2.0 shifts content-safety vocabulary from 2.55 to 10.37 hits per 100 tokens, while a magnitude-matched random direction produces 1.13-2.16; the model continues to refuse but switches register from meta-style ("as a language model...") to content-style ("this would be harmful"). The same register-injection effect reproduces qualitatively in Gemma-2-2B-IT at layer 12 (content vocabulary 1.72 -> 6.37 at alpha = 1.0, vs. random control 1.35), with a narrower coherent-injection window than in 9B. The two directions are not symmetric: the B2 -> harmful intervention produces a much smaller register effect, and across ablation, sufficiency, and injection B1's causal effects are consistently larger than B2's. We frame this asymmetry as part of the finding: B1 appears to encode both category detection and refusal-vocabulary information, while B2 encodes primarily category detection. We frame the contribution as identifying category-aligned components related to the Arditi-style difference-of-means direction that play distinct functional roles in refusal register.

title: Augmenting Pretrained Language Models with N-gram Embeddings through Incremental Training
summary: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.

title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
summary: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 main tables, and 1 supplementary table
summary: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
summary: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Results of the registered tests that need the ICLR 2027 decisions will be added after 16 December 2026
summary: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
summary: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.

title: MetaAct: Self-Evolving Executable Action Constraints for Embodied Language Agents
summary: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.

title: LEAF-OPD: Learning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation
summary: LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.

title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
